subject: biology
title: Mitosis and meiosis
summary: Why and how cells divide by mitosis and meiosis, how the two processes compare, and how meiosis creates genetic variation.
body:
Every one of your trillions of cells came from a single fertilised egg, and cells keep dividing to grow you, heal cuts and replace worn-out skin. Cells divide in two different ways. **Mitosis** makes identical copies for growth and repair, while **meiosis** makes sex cells that are all genetically different, which is why siblings (apart from identical twins) never look exactly alike.

## Think of it like this

### Mitosis is like photocopying a full set of notes for a friend

Before you can give a friend a copy of your notes, you have to copy every page. That's **interphase**, when the cell **replicates its DNA** so each chromosome becomes two identical **sister chromatids**. In **mitosis**, the copies are shared out so each new cell gets one of each page: two complete, identical sets. Chromosomes line up in the middle in **metaphase**, like students lining up in single file at assembly, and in **anaphase** the **spindle fibres** pull the sister chromatids to opposite ends. **Cytokinesis** then splits the cell into two **diploid** daughter cells with 46 chromosomes each.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* when you photocopy, you keep the original and give away the copy, but in mitosis the original cell no longer exists; it becomes the two daughter cells, each holding one old and one newly made DNA strand in every chromatid.

### Meiosis is like dealing a hand from two decks of cards

Imagine you have two decks, one from mum and one from dad, each with 23 matching cards. To make a **gamete**, you take one card from each matching pair, giving a hand of 23 cards: **haploid**. Whether you take mum's or dad's version of card 1 has nothing to do with card 2, which is **independent assortment**, giving about 8.4 million possible hands. In **meiosis I**, the **homologous** pairs are separated; in **meiosis II**, the sister chromatids are separated, ending with **four genetically different** cells.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* cards stay exactly as printed, but real chromosomes can swap sections first. That's **crossing over**, like cutting mum's and dad's versions of the same card in the same place and taping the halves together, making brand new combinations of alleles that didn't exist before.

### Halving the chromosome number is like two halves making a whole team

A footy team needs a full side on the field. If two full teams merged every time a new team formed, the numbers would double each season. In the same way, a sperm (n = 23) and an egg (n = 23) each bring half, so the zygote has 46. **Meiosis** halving the number is what keeps it at 46 generation after generation.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* any two half-teams could join up, but a sperm and egg must each bring exactly one chromosome from every one of the 23 pairs. Missing or extra chromosomes can cause problems, such as trisomy 21.

### In real life

Every time a graze on your knee heals over, mitosis is making new identical skin cells. Meiosis, with crossing over and random fertilisation, is why you and your siblings look different even though you share the same parents, unless you are identical twins.

## Key ideas

### Before any division: interphase

A cell spends most of its life in **interphase**, the stage between divisions. During interphase the cell grows, does its normal jobs and, importantly, **replicates its DNA**. After replication, each chromosome is made of two identical **sister chromatids** joined at a **centromere**. The chromosome number has not changed (a human cell still has 46 chromosomes), but there is now twice as much DNA, ready to share out.

### Mitosis: making identical cells

**Mitosis** is the division of the nucleus that produces **two genetically identical diploid daughter cells**. It is followed by **cytokinesis**, the splitting of the cytoplasm into two cells. Mitosis is used for:

- **growth** (e.g. a baby growing into an adult)
- **repair** and replacement (e.g. healing a cut, replacing red blood cells)
- **asexual reproduction** in some organisms (e.g. yeast, many plants)

Mitosis has four stages. A common memory aid is **PMAT**.

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Prophase** | Chromosomes coil up and become visible. The nuclear membrane breaks down. Spindle fibres start to form. |
| **Metaphase** | Chromosomes line up in single file along the middle (equator) of the cell, attached to spindle fibres at their centromeres. |
| **Anaphase** | Spindle fibres pull the sister chromatids apart to opposite ends (poles) of the cell. |
| **Telophase** | A new nuclear membrane forms around each set of chromosomes. The chromosomes uncoil. |

Because each daughter cell receives one chromatid from every chromosome, both cells get an **exact copy** of the original DNA. In humans, a cell with 46 chromosomes produces two cells with 46 chromosomes each.

### Meiosis: making gametes

**Meiosis** is the type of division that produces **gametes** (sperm and eggs in animals; pollen and ovules in flowering plants). It happens only in the sex organs (testes and ovaries in humans). Meiosis involves **two divisions** one after the other, and produces **four haploid cells** that are all **genetically different**.

**Meiosis I** (separates homologous pairs):

- Homologous chromosomes pair up side by side. While paired, they may swap sections of DNA (crossing over; see below).
- The pairs line up in the middle of the cell.
- The two chromosomes of each pair are pulled to opposite poles.
- Two cells form, each with **half the chromosome number** (23 in humans), though each chromosome still has two chromatids.

**Meiosis II** (separates sister chromatids, much like mitosis):

- In each of the two cells, chromosomes line up in the middle.
- Sister chromatids are pulled apart.
- The result is **four haploid cells**, each with 23 single chromosomes in humans.

Halving the chromosome number is essential. When a sperm (n = 23) fertilises an egg (n = 23), the zygote has 46 chromosomes. Without meiosis, the number would double every generation.

### Comparing mitosis and meiosis

| Feature | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Growth, repair, asexual reproduction | Making gametes for sexual reproduction |
| Where (humans) | Body cells all over the body | Testes and ovaries only |
| Number of divisions | 1 | 2 |
| Number of cells produced | 2 | 4 |
| Chromosome number of new cells | Diploid (2n), same as parent: 46 | Haploid (n), half of parent: 23 |
| Genetically identical? | Yes, identical to parent and each other | No, all different |
| Homologous chromosomes pair up? | No | Yes, in meiosis I |
| Crossing over? | No | Yes |

### Why meiosis creates variation

Three processes shuffle genetic information.

**1. Crossing over.** In meiosis I, when homologous chromosomes are paired, their chromatids can break and swap matching sections. This creates chromosomes with **new combinations of alleles** that did not exist in either parent's chromosomes before. For example, a chromosome that carried alleles for brown hair and freckles from Mum might swap a section with Dad's chromosome and end up with brown hair and no freckles.

**2. Independent assortment.** When homologous pairs line up in meiosis I, the way each pair faces is random. Whether the maternal or paternal chromosome of pair 1 goes to a particular pole has nothing to do with which way pair 2 goes. With 23 pairs, one person can make 2²³, or about 8.4 million, different combinations of chromosomes, even before crossing over is counted.

**3. Random fertilisation.** This happens after meiosis, but adds even more variation: any one of millions of genetically different sperm can fertilise the egg.

Variation matters because a population with lots of genetic differences is more likely to have some individuals who survive changes such as new diseases or a changing climate. This is the raw material for natural selection.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: Chromosome numbers

**Question:** A dog body cell has 78 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in (a) a cell made by mitosis and (b) a dog sperm cell?

**(a)** Mitosis keeps the number the same: **78**.

**(b)** A sperm is made by meiosis, which halves the number: 78 ÷ 2 = **39**.

**Check:** sperm (39) + egg (39) = 78 in the puppy's first cell, which matches.

### Example 2: Identifying a stage from a description

**Question:** A student describes a cell under the microscope: "Chromosomes are lined up along the middle of the cell in pairs, with homologous chromosomes side by side." Is this mitosis or meiosis, and which stage?

**Step 1:** In mitosis, chromosomes line up in single file, not in pairs.

**Step 2:** Homologous chromosomes lining up in pairs only happens in **meiosis I**.

**Answer:** Metaphase of meiosis I.

### Example 3: Counting combinations

**Question:** An organism has a diploid number of 6 (three homologous pairs). Ignoring crossing over, how many different chromosome combinations can its gametes have?

**Step 1:** Number of pairs n = 6 ÷ 2 = 3.

**Step 2:** Combinations = 2ⁿ = 2³ = **8**.

## Common mistakes

- **Saying mitosis makes gametes.** Gametes are made by meiosis; mitosis makes body cells.
- **Mixing up chromatids and chromosomes when counting.** Count centromeres: each centromere is one chromosome, whether it has one or two chromatids.
- **Thinking DNA replicates between meiosis I and meiosis II.** DNA is copied once only, in interphase before meiosis I.
- **Saying meiosis cells are "half as big".** They have half the chromosome number, not half the size.
- **Forgetting crossing over happens in meiosis I only**, between homologous chromosomes, not in mitosis.

## Exam tips

- Comparison questions are very common. Use a table and give matching points side by side (purpose, number of cells, chromosome number, identical or not).
- To earn marks for "explain how meiosis causes variation", name the process (crossing over or independent assortment) **and** say what it does (new combinations of alleles).
- Be able to work out chromosome numbers for any species given its diploid number.

## Tips to remember

- **"IPMAT"** – Interphase (DNA copied), then mitosis: Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase.
- **A made-up sound-alike: mitosis = "my toes"** – it grows and repairs your body cells. **Meiosis = "meet"** – it makes gametes that meet at fertilisation.
- **Numbers to remember: mitosis 1 division → 2 identical diploid cells; meiosis 2 divisions → 4 different haploid cells.** Human cells: 46 → 46 and 46 → 23.
- **Count centromeres to count chromosomes,** whether each one has one chromatid or two.
- **Three shufflers of variation: crossing over, independent assortment, random fertilisation.** With 23 pairs, 2²³ is about 8.4 million combinations before crossing over is even counted.
- **DNA is copied once only,** in interphase before meiosis I, not again between meiosis I and II.

## Key terms

- **Interphase** — the stage between divisions when the cell grows and copies its DNA.
- **Mitosis** — nuclear division producing two identical diploid cells.
- **Cytokinesis** — division of the cytoplasm to form separate cells.
- **Spindle fibres** — protein fibres that move chromosomes during division.
- **Meiosis** — two divisions producing four genetically different haploid gametes.
- **Crossing over** — swapping of DNA sections between homologous chromosomes in meiosis I.
- **Independent assortment** — the random way homologous pairs line up and separate in meiosis I.
- **Zygote** — the diploid cell formed when a sperm fertilises an egg.

## Summary

- DNA is copied in interphase, so each chromosome has two sister chromatids before division.
- Mitosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) makes two identical diploid cells for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.
- Meiosis has two divisions and makes four different haploid gametes.
- Halving the chromosome number keeps it constant across generations after fertilisation.
- Crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation create genetic variation.

questions.prompt: Which process produces the cells used to repair a cut on your hand?
questions.explanation: Repair needs new cells identical to the old ones, which mitosis provides. Meiosis is tempting because it is also cell division, but it makes genetically different gametes.

questions.prompt: In which stage of mitosis are sister chromatids pulled to opposite ends of the cell?
questions.explanation: In anaphase the spindle fibres pull sister chromatids apart to the poles. In metaphase the chromosomes are only lined up in the middle, not yet separated.

questions.prompt: A horse body cell contains 64 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in a horse egg cell?
questions.explanation: Egg cells are made by meiosis, which halves the diploid number: 64 ÷ 2 = 32. Option C (16) results from halving twice, a mistake made by thinking each meiotic division halves the number again.

questions.prompt: Which feature is true of meiosis but NOT of mitosis?

options.B: Homologous chromosomes pair up and may cross over

questions.explanation: Pairing of homologous chromosomes and crossing over happen only in meiosis I. Option C is tempting, but DNA is replicated in interphase before both mitosis and meiosis.

questions.prompt: Why is it important that gametes are haploid?

options.A: So the zygote formed at fertilisation has the normal diploid number
options.B: So gametes are small enough to move
options.C: So gametes are identical to the parent's body cells
options.D: So gametes can divide by mitosis to form an embryo straight away

questions.explanation: Two haploid gametes (n + n) join to restore the diploid number (2n), keeping chromosome number constant between generations. Option B confuses chromosome number with cell size.

questions.prompt: How does crossing over increase genetic variation?

options.A: It doubles the number of chromosomes in each gamete
options.B: It creates brand new genes that neither parent had
options.C: It swaps sections between homologous chromosomes, producing new combinations of alleles
options.D: It makes all four gametes identical

questions.explanation: Crossing over exchanges matching DNA sections between maternal and paternal chromosomes, creating new combinations of existing alleles. Option B is a common misconception: crossing over reshuffles alleles, it does not invent new genes (that requires mutation).

questions.prompt: A species has a diploid number of 8. Ignoring crossing over, how many different chromosome combinations are possible in its gametes due to independent assortment?
questions.explanation: 2n = 8, so there are 4 homologous pairs, giving 2⁴ = 16 combinations. Option B (2⁸ = 256) uses the diploid number instead of the number of pairs.

questions.prompt: A cell is seen with 23 chromosomes, each made of two chromatids, lining up in single file along the middle of the cell. The organism is human. Which stage is this most likely to be?
questions.explanation: Only 23 chromosomes means the cell has already completed meiosis I; single-file lining up of chromosomes with two chromatids fits metaphase of meiosis II. Option A is tempting because the line-up looks like mitosis, but a human cell in mitosis would have 46 chromosomes.
